newsitem.title: UK: CBI wants prudent British budget, but will they get it?.
newsitem.headline: CBI wants prudent British budget, but will they get it?.

text.p: Britain's top employers group the Confederation of British Industry on Wednesday called for a British budget offering only minimal tax cuts but its plea may fall on deaf ears with an election looming, analysts said.

The CBI on Wednesday, urged the government to trim its real spending target by two billion pounds ($3.1 billion) at November's budget and opt for tax cuts of only about one billion pounds in order to ensure public deficits head lower.
But economists said tax cuts to the tune of at least three billion pounds were more likely although Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would probably not break the bank.

"What we want is a budget which delivers a sound fiscal position," said Andrew Buxton, chairman of Barclays Bank Plc and the CBI's economic affairs committee. "The Chancellor should have prudence as a watchword."

The Conservative government must call an election by May 1997 and trails the opposition Labour Party badly in the polls. As a result, Clarke is under pressure to cut taxes, cut interest rates and generally do anything he can to improve Tory fortunes.
The CBI said the key economic point for Clarke was that Britain's public deficit, or public sector borrowing requirement, had consistently overshot targets in recent years.
CBI director-general Adair Turner said the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) was the one negative part of a generally positive economic backdrop and needed to be addressed.

But Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley, said Clarke could cut income taxes by about three billion pounds on November 26 and still produce a lower forecast for the PSBR if he got his sums right.
Three billion pounds could take 1.5 or even two percentage points off the basic rate of income tax, now at 24 percent.

Gardiner said the Treasury's projection for a public sector borrowing requirement of 23 billion pounds in 1997/98 was probably overcautious as the economy seems set to grow quite robustly for the rest of this year and next.
If Clarke and his Treasury ministers could find some extra cuts in the budgets of government departments, and Gardiner thought they could, tax cuts can be justified.

Here again, the CBI begged to differ. Turner said the spending cuts demanded by his organisation should come out of the government's contingency reserve -- a fund for emergency spending -- not departmental budgets.
"Further reductions (in departments' spending)...will not be easy," he said, adding that the CBI did not wish to see spending cut on education and training or capital infrastructure.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, agreed with the CBI that a neutral or even tight budget was needed, given the size of Britain's public sector deficit.

But he said reasonably substantial tax cuts could still be afforded. "We think we will see tax cuts of several billion pounds, but given the state of public finances they will have to be offset by planned spending cuts."
Loynes said that if push came to shove, and Clarke had to choose between tax or interest rate cuts for maximum political effect, then he would probably opt for the fiscal side.
"The tax cuts would have the highest impact, particularly in headline terms," Loynes said. "Interest rates are already at very low levels."
Gardiner agreed. "More people pay tax than have mortgages, so income tax cuts would seem to be the political favourite."

The CBI said any tax cuts should be aimed at reducing the burden it the lower end of the income scale. It also argued for measures to assist small and medium-sized enterprises to be prioritised. ($1=.6392 Pound) REUTER
